correctness.rationale: Maga–Tóth Theorem 1.2 uses N for total particle count; N=Kn gives exactly the frozen a.s. normalization and the 1/K factor at each fixed a. Every cut objective is strictly convex and diverges at both endpoints, so its unique interior minimizer depends smoothly on a, including in the moving first gap. Differentiation at stationarity yields −1/[K(z_m+a)²]; the locations are strictly ordered by their gaps, and the denominators positive. Thus pair differences strictly decrease and maximizing indices cannot fall. At a tie the left and right derivatives of the finite envelope are respectively the least and greatest active slopes, so the strict order gives an upward jump. For the special family, at a=1 the middle value is 4/3 and the two trials give outside values ≤19/15. Monotonicity preserves C₂>C₃ to the left, while C₁≥1/a and C₂ is bounded there, giving the unique crossing. With three species, reflection at equal gaps and strict decrease settle both sides, so four species are minimal for a smallest-gap mismatch. Independently using only two fixed rational trial points (−483/1000 and 501/1000) and F''≥32/gap³, exact outward-rounded bounds on C₁−C₂ in units of 10⁻⁸ were [18551,18635] at 467/500 and [−91926,−91876] at 187/200. The supplied script was inspected, not run. The proof is about fixed-speed asymptotic coefficients, not finite-N or uniform-in-a stochastic limits.

value.rationale: The strict derivative order is a structural constraint on the entire cut envelope, not just one optimized value. It yields a global no-reentrance rule, strict corners, and a certified minimal-species counterexample to identifying the bottleneck by the smallest gap. The four-species phase diagram is a motivated sharp example of that constraint rather than an arbitrary scalar computation.
